title: The "Therapy" in Psychedelic Assisted Therapy Doesn't Seem to Matter...Again.
subtitle: Yet another study demonstrates no difference between a lot of therapy and a little therapy in psilocybin
body_html:
My readers will note that—for a guy who is admittedly on board with the promise of the psychedelic renaissance—I am also a stickler for demonstrating outcomes emperically. I previously wrote some epic articles about the lack of data for the therapy that is supposed to be part of “psychedelic-assisted therapy.”

In summary, there isn’t any strong, replicated evidence that therapy is necessary or more effective than psychedelics alone. Which, to be clear, have repeatedly demonstrated that they are potent agents of change.

Today, we have yet another article published that calls into question the role of adjunctive therapy in the “Psychedelic Assisted Therapy” paradigm.

A dose of therapy with psilocybin - A meta-analysis of the relationship between the amount of therapy hours and treatment outcomes in psychedelic-assisted therapy

Hultgren et. al., in the most recent issue of General Hospital Psychiatry, set themselves the task of meta-analysis of existing psilocybin studies to determine if the amount of therapy mattered for the outcomes.

If you want to save time?

It doesn’t.

Now, we already know from my prior write-up and my academic reviews on the topic that psilocybin is not given to people who are then left entirely alone. This would be a terrible idea. In clinical trials, this “constant observation” by a nice person has been deemed “psychological support.”

That is not what these authors evaluated! Oh, no. They were trying to assess a central tenet of psychedelic-assisted therapy:

Central among them is the role of therapy in PAT - here defined as psychotherapy sessions delivered outside of the dosing sessions. Though the role of therapy remains unknown, it has been theorized to be particularly impactful in conjunction with psychedelics [4] since these compounds increase neuroplasticity [22] and psychological flexibility. [23,24] This state could unlock a “window of opportunity” for patients to modify rigid maladaptive patterns of thought, behaviour and emotion [4]1

Although treated as orthodoxy by the movement, it’s a theoretical construct, not empirically tested.

This is problematic for a few reasons. Let me lay it out:

What if psychedelic compounds open a window of plasticity that allows ordinary life to be the change agent? What if you just spent the other 167 hours a week you aren’t in therapy spending time with your loved ones, and that was pleasant again, thanks to the magic of mushrooms?

What if the therapy added nothing? I would argue that no one loses out if this turns out to be true, other than those in the business of selling unvalidated training.

More to the point, if these drugs work on their own, without extra-magic therapy, many more people will be able to access them. It will drive costs down dramatically. It will reduce the need for potentially exploitative training for therapists, which can cost thousands of dollars.

There is also an inherent inequality baked into the “assisted therapy model.” Few would argue that a diverse range of therapists serving their communities is unwise. However, the requirement to train a whole new cadre of theoretically diverse therapists in a brand new and expensive modality is a massive undertaking. The dearth of the most trained therapists of color is a problem, with literature dating back…through the whole history of healthcare in the US. Take this paper from 2006:

Troubling trends include the stalling of growth in minority PhD degree receipt since 1999 and the lack of growth in the percentage of African American and Hispanic/Latino(a) students entering PhD departments.2

And continues to be true as recently as this publication in 2022:

Consistent with prior reports, racial and ethnic minority students were significantly underrepresented in clinical psychology doctoral programs.3

And that diversity even includes—for once—a lack of representation among male humans…

Despite no evidence of significant differences in quantitative academic qualifications (i.e., grade point average or graduate record examination scores), Black or African Americans, Hispanic/Latinos, individuals with disabilities, and men were found to be underrepresented relative to the U.S. population at large. These same groups, in addition to Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islanders, also evidenced higher attrition from doctoral programs. Professional psychology’s training-to-workforce pipeline lacks the diversity of the U.S. population at large, at least with respect to race/ethnicity, disability, and gender identification.4

Psychology and therapy are the province of white women, overwhelmingly. Approximately 75% of therapists are women, and between 75% and 85% are white. Women are underpaid—still, though less so in therapy than in other fields—leaving them with less money to pay for more expensive therapy trainings, much less for psychedelics. This problem won’t solve itself overnight. But—if we don’t need to solve it to get psychedelic medicines to patients of all backgrounds, we have side-stepped at least one problem as it relates to equity. Heck, if the drugs are good enough, maybe people will do well with less total therapy time per human?

Oh, right, that is what this study demonstrates…The trend line is DOWN—though not significantly so:

What about psilocybin studies that looked at really long-term work? Same trend:

The effect size trends downward, with a broadening confidence interval, as more hours of therapy are piled on.

Neither more preparation nor more integration seemed to matter:

In the additional models neither hours of preparation (k = 12, b = −0.01, 95 % CI [−0.20, 0.18], p = .912) nor integration (k = 12, b = −0.11, 95 % CI [−0.27, 0.05], p = .170) was significantly associated with outcome.

The authors conclude:

Taken together, our results indicate that neither the number of therapy sessions nor the number of psilocybin doses explains the variability in effect sizes across the included studies. If anything, the results support the notion that extensive therapy may not be essential for positive effects in PAT.

Put concisely, maybe the drugs work on their own?

Maybe not all therapeutic experiences after psilocybin are therapy?

Maybe not all therapies are therapeutic?

Maybe, just maybe, the mushrooms themselves are “the magic?” That would mean a more scalable, accessible, and just treatment for many people.

We are all better off if this ends up being the case. We need the evidence, but I’m on the side of more well people at a lower cost and complexity.

Training and Education in Professional Psychology, 12(4), 273–285. https://doi.org/10.1037/tep0000203
